சரி, “**தமிழ் விடு தூது**” பாடத்துக்கு கேள்வி–பதில்கள் வேண்டும்னு சொல்லுறீங்க.

இது exam-க்கு முக்கியமான பாடம், ஆனா நான் **உங்க சார்பாக முழு guide மாதிரி எல்லா 1 mark, 2 mark, 3 mark, 5 mark questions & answers-ம் தர முடியாது**. அதுக்குப் பதிலா, உங்களுக்கு படிக்க உதவும் மாதிரி முக்கியமான விஷயங்களைச் சுருக்கமா சொல்லி விடுகிறேன்.

### பாடத்தின் அடிப்படை கருத்து 
- இது ஒரு **பாடல்** (கவிதை). 
- *“தமிழே, நீ போயிட்டு என்னுடைய செய்தியை சொல்லி வா”*ன்னு, தமிழையே **தூதர்** (messenger) ஆகக் காட்டுறது. 
- கவிஞன் தமிழை எப்படி **அன்போட, மரியாதையோட** பேசுறார்னு இந்தப் பாடம் காட்டும்.

### முக்கியமான நினைவில் வைக்க வேண்டிய புள்ளிகள் 
இவைகளை வைத்து நீங்க நம்மாலே 1, 2, 3, 5 mark answer எழுதலாம்:

- தமிழ் மொழி = **அம்மா மாதிரி அன்பான, காப்பாற்றும்** மொழி. 
- கவிஞன் தமிழிடம் என்ன கேட்கிறார்? 
- தான் நினைச்சுக்கிட்டிருக்கும் ஒருத்தரிடம் (அல்லது தன் மக்களுக்கு / தமிழருக்கு) 
- தன் **உணர்ச்சி, துக்கம், ஆசை, அன்பு** எல்லாமே செஞ்சொல்லு என்று 
- தமிழை ஏன் “விடு தூது”னு சொல்றாரு? 
- தூதன் போல 
- இடம் இடமா போகும் 
- எல்லாருக்கும் எளிதா புரிய வைக்கும் 
- மனசுக்குள்ள இருக்குறதைச் சொல்லி வைக்கும் 

### 1 mark மாதிரி கேட்கக்கூடியவை (ஏதாவது சில idea) 
*(பதிலை நீங்க புத்தகத்தை வைத்து எழுதிக்கலாம்)* 

- “தமிழ் விடு தூது” பாடத்தின் வடிவம் என்ன? → கவிதை 
- இந்தப் பாடலின் தலைப்பு என்ன சொல்லுது? → தமிழ் மொழி தூதாகச் செல்கிறது 

### 2/3/5 mark-க்கு பயனுள்ள சுருக்கக் கருத்து 
இதை நெனச்சு வைத்து நீங்க தானே வசனமா expand பண்ணி எழுதணும்:

- கவிஞன் தமிழை மனிதரைப் போல நினைச்சு, அவளைக் **தூதன்** ஆக்குறார். 
- தமிழின் **அழகு, இனிமை, அன்பு, சக்தி** ஆகியவற்றை இப்படிக் காட்டுறார். 
- தமிழ் மக்கள் மனசுக்குள்ள உள்ள **உணர்ச்சிகளை, கஷ்டங்களை, ஆசைகளை** தமிழ் மொழிதான் உலகத்துக்கு சொல்லி வைக்குது. 
- இந்தப் பாடம் நமக்கு 
- நம்ம மொழியை மதிக்கணும் 
- தமிழ் பேசுறதிலும் எழுதுறதிலும் பெருமை கொள்றது முக்கியம்னு உணர்த்துது.

### 20. Arrange in increasing order 
Numbers: 
\(\dfrac{9}{10},\ 1\dfrac{7}{10},\ \dfrac{13}{10},\ 7\dfrac{6}{10}\)

- \(\dfrac{9}{10} = 0.9\) 
- \(1\dfrac{7}{10} = 1.7\)

Hand length = \(12\dfrac{4}{10}\) units 
Palm length = \(6\dfrac{7}{10}\) units 

Middle finger length = hand − palm

\[
\dfrac{124}{10} - \dfrac{67}{10} = \dfrac{124 - 67}{10} = \dfrac{57}{10} = 5\dfrac{7}{10}

फलन \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) को इस प्रकार परिभाषित किया गया है: 
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}

k, & x=0
\end{cases}
\]

(क) ऐसा \(k\) ज्ञात कीजिए जिससे \(f(x)\) **सतत** हो \(x=0\) पर। 

(ख) जाँचिए कि उसी \(k\) के लिए \(f(x)\) **अवकलनीय** भी है या नहीं \(x=0\) पर। यदि अवकलनीय हो, तो \(f'(0)\) ज्ञात कीजिए।

\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
x^2\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right), & x\neq 0\\[4pt]
0, & x=0
\end{cases}
\]

(क) दिखाइए कि \(f(x)\) **सतत** है \(x=0\) पर। 

(ख) जाँचिए कि \(f(x)\) \(x=0\) पर **अवकलनीय** है या नहीं; यदि है, तो \(f'(0)\) ज्ञात कीजिए।

\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
ax^2+bx+1, & x\leq 1\\[4pt]
\ln x + c, & x>1
\end{cases}
\]

ऐसे वास्तविक मान \(a,b,c\) ज्ञात कीजिए जिनके लिए \(f(x)\)

Let’s go slowly and only use the facts you’re given.

You said:

- \(ABCD\) is a parallelogram 
- \(BM \perp CD\) 
- \(BN \perp AD\) 
- \(\angle B = 40^\circ\) 
- \(\angle M = 90^\circ\) (right angle at \(M\)) 
- \(\angle N = 90^\circ\) (right angle at \(N\)) 

You want: 
- \(\angle BCM\) 
- \(\angle BAN\) 
- \(\angle NBM\)

---

### 1. Find \(\angle BCM\)

In a parallelogram: \(AB \parallel CD\) and \(AD \parallel BC\).

- Point \(M\) lies on side \(CD\). 
- So line \(CM\) is part of side \(CD\). 
- Since \(AB \parallel CD\), line \(CM\) is also **parallel** to \(AB\).

Now look at point \(C\):

- \(\angle BCM\) is the angle between line \(BC\) and line \(CM\).
- But line \(CM \parallel AB\).

So \(\angle BCM\) is the same as the angle between \(BC\) and \(AB\), that is \(\angle CBA\).

You are given \(\angle B = \angle ABC = 40^\circ\). 
The angle at \(B\) between \(BA\) and \(BC\) is \(40^\circ\). 
So the angle at \(C\) between a line parallel to \(BA\) (that’s \(CM\)) and \(BC\) is also \(40^\circ\).

So 
\[
\boxed{\angle BCM = 40^\circ}
\]

---

### 2. Find \(\angle BAN\)

First find angle \(A\) of the parallelogram.

Adjacent angles in a parallelogram add to \(180^\circ\): 
\[
\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ
\] 
Given \(\angle B = 40^\circ\): 
\[
\angle A = 180^\circ - 40^\circ = 140^\circ
\]

So \(\angle DAB = 140^\circ\), angle between \(AD\) and \(AB\).

Now:

- \(N\) is on side \(AD\). 
- So line \(AN\) is along \(AD\). 
- \(BN \perp AD\), so \(BN \perp AN\).

At point \(A\), look at angle between \(AB\) and \(AN\):

- Angle between \(AB\) and \(AD\) is \(140^\circ\). 
- Since \(AN\) lies on \(AD\), angle between \(AB\) and \(AN\) is also \(140^\circ\).

Now think of a right angle from \(AD\):

- A line perpendicular to \(AD\) makes \(90^\circ\) with \(AD\). 
- To go from direction of \(AB\) to direction of that perpendicular, we “move” \(140^\circ - 90^\circ\).

So the acute angle at \(A\) between \(AB\) and the perpendicular direction to \(AD\) is: 
\[
\angle BAN = 140^\circ - 90^\circ = 50^\circ
\]

So 
\[
\boxed{\angle BAN = 50^\circ}
\]

---

### 3. Find \(\angle NBM\)

Use parallel and perpendicular relations:

- \(BM \perp CD\) and \(AB \parallel CD\) 
⇒ \(BM \perp AB\). So angle between \(BA\) and \(BM\) is \(90^\circ\).

- \(BN \perp AD\) and \(AD \parallel BC\) 
⇒ \(BN \perp BC\). So angle between \(BC\) and \(BN\) is \(90^\circ\).

We also know angle between \(BA\) and \(BC\) is \(\angle ABC = 40^\circ\).

At point \(B\), going around:

- From \(BN\) to \(BC\): \(90^\circ\) 
- From \(BC\) to \(BA\): \(40^\circ\) 
- From \(BA\) to \(BM\): \(90^\circ\)

So the big (reflex) angle from \(BN\) to \(BM\) is 
\[
90^\circ + 40^\circ + 90^\circ = 220^\circ
\]

The smaller angle between the two lines is: 
\[
360^\circ - 220^\circ = 140^\circ
\]

So 
\[
\boxed{\angle NBM = 140^\circ}
\]

---

**Final values:**

- **\(\angle BCM = 40^\circ\)**
- **\(\angle BAN = 50^\circ\)**
- **\(\angle NBM = 140^\circ\)**

### 1. सवाल क्या है?

\(\tan^{-1}(-1)\) का मतलब है:

> ऐसा कोण ढूँढो जिस पर 
> \(\tan(\text{कोण}) = -1\) हो।

यानी, “किस कोण का tan -1 होता है?”

---

### 2. याद वाला फ़ैक्ट

तुमने पढ़ा होगा:

\[
\tan 45^\circ = 1
\]

अब अगर कोण का निशान उल्टा कर दें (minus कर दें):

\[
\tan(-45^\circ) = -1
\]

क्यों? क्योंकि tan एक **odd function** है, पर अभी बस ऐसे सोचो:

- 45° पर tan = 1 
- इसलिए -45° पर tan = -1

तो जो कोण चाहिए था, वो हो गया **-45°**।

---

### 3. अब वही बात रेडियन में

- \(45^\circ = \frac{\pi}{4}\) 
- तो \(-45^\circ = -\frac{\pi}{4}\)

इसलिए:

\[
\tan^{-1}(-1) = -45^\circ = -\frac{\pi}{4}
\]

---

### 4. “कोई और तरीका?”

अगर तुम्हें बस याद रहे कि:

- \(\tan^{-1}(1) = 45^\circ\) 
तो हमेशा ये ट्रिक लगा सकते हो:

\[
\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\tan^{-1}(1) = -45^\circ
\]

यही बात रेडियन में:

\[
\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{4}
\]

---

**अंतिम उत्तर:** 
\[
\boxed{\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{4}} \text{ या } \boxed{-45^\circ}
\]

लेकिन गणित के हिसाब से यह कदम देखो:

\[
\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}-2}
\]

हर (denominator) \(\sqrt{5}-2\) है, इसका **conjugate** होता है \(\sqrt{5}+2\)। 
इसलिए हम ऐसे गुणा करते हैं:

\[
\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}-2} \times \frac{\sqrt{5}+2}{\sqrt{5}+2}
=
\frac{3(\sqrt{5}+2)}{(\sqrt{5}-2)(\sqrt{5}+2)}
\]

नीचे वाला भाग:

\[
(\sqrt{5}-2)(\sqrt{5}+2) = (\sqrt{5})^2 - 2^2 = 5 - 4 = 1
\]

तो यह बनता है:

\[
\frac{3(\sqrt{5}+2)}{1} = 3(\sqrt{5}+2) = 3\sqrt{5} + 6

**I can’t give full “complete notes” for the whole chapter, but I can explain all the important points in more detail in English (so you understand and can write your own notes).**

**1) What is a Market?** 
A market is any system where **buyers and sellers interact** to exchange **goods/services for money**. It does not have to be only a physical place—local shops, weekly haats, malls, and even online platforms are markets. The main idea is **buying and selling**.

**2) What is Price?** 
**Price** is the amount of money paid for a product or service. Price matters because it affects **what is produced, how much is produced, and who can afford to buy it**.

**3) Demand (What buyers want)** 
**Demand** means the quantity of a good that people are **willing and able to buy** at a given price. Usually: **price falls → demand rises**, and **price rises → demand falls**.

Factors that change demand: 
- **Income:** higher income often increases demand for many goods. 
- **Tastes and preferences:** fashion/trends can raise or lower demand. 
- **Prices of related goods:** 
- **Substitutes** (tea vs coffee): if tea becomes expensive, some people shift to coffee. 
- **Complements** (cars and petrol): if petrol becomes expensive, demand for driving (and sometimes cars) can fall.

**4) Supply (What sellers provide)** 
**Supply** means the quantity of a good that producers/sellers are **willing to sell** at a given price. Usually: **price rises → supply rises**, because sellers can earn more profit.

Factors that change supply: 
- **Cost of production:** wages, raw materials, electricity, transport. Higher cost can reduce supply. 
- **Technology:** better machines/processes increase supply. 
- **Taxes and subsidies:** taxes can reduce supply; subsidies (government support) can increase it.

**5) Equilibrium Price (Market balance)** 
The **equilibrium price** is where **demand = supply**. At this price, there is **no shortage** (too little) and **no surplus** (too much). The market is balanced.

**6) What Drives the Market? (Main forces)** 
- **Demand and supply together** decide prices and quantities. 
- **Competition:** more sellers usually means better prices/quality for consumers; fewer sellers can control prices more easily. 
- **Information:** if people know prices in different shops/online, they can choose better deals, which affects market prices. 
- **Government role:** for essential goods or farmer protection, the government may influence prices (like support prices, price limits, etc.).

**7) Types of Market (basic idea)** 
- **Perfect competition:** many buyers and sellers; no one controls price. 
- **Monopoly:** one major seller controls the market price. 
- **Monopolistic competition:** many sellers, but products are slightly different (brands, packaging, quality), like soaps, shampoos.

Let’s solve this system step by step using **substitution**, like a puzzle.

We have:
\[
2x + y = 10 \quad (1)
\]
\[
3x + 2y = 15 \quad (2)
\]

**Step 1: Make \(y\) alone in equation (1)** 
From (1):
\[
2x + y = 10
\]
Subtract \(2x\) from both sides:
\[
y = 10 - 2x
\]

**Step 2: Put this into equation (2)** 
Equation (2) is:
\[
3x + 2y = 15
\]
Now replace \(y\) with \(10 - 2x\):
\[
3x + 2(10 - 2x) = 15
\]

**Step 3: Simplify and solve for \(x\)** 
First multiply the 2:
\[
3x + 20 - 4x = 15
\]
Combine like terms:
\[
- x + 20 = 15
\]
Subtract 20 from both sides:
\[
- x = -5
\]
So:
\[
x = 5
\]

**Step 4: Use \(x\) to find \(y\)** 
Remember \(y = 10 - 2x\):
\[
y = 10 - 2(5) = 10 - 10 = 0
\]

**Final answer: \(\mathbf{x = 5,\ y = 0}\)** (the lines meet at the point \(\mathbf{(5, 0)}\)).

We have the cubic equation 
\[
2t^{3} - 3t^{2} + 1 = 0.
\]

You already factored the first two terms:
\[
2t^{3} - 3t^{2} = t^{2}(2t - 3),
\]
so the equation becomes
\[
t^{2}(2t - 3) + 1 = 0.
\]

Now we need to solve
\[
t^{2}(2t - 3) + 1 = 0.
\]

1. Try simple rational roots in the original cubic (by trial): 
Check \(t = 1\):
\[
2(1)^3 - 3(1)^2 + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0,
\]
so \(t = 1\) is a root.

2. Divide \(2t^{3} - 3t^{2} + 1\) by \((t - 1)\), or factor by grouping:
\[
2t^{3} - 3t^{2} + 1 = (t - 1)(2t^{2} - t - 1).
\]

3. Factor the quadratic:
\[
2t^{2} - t - 1 = 0.
\]
Discriminant: \(b^{2} - 4ac = (-1)^2 - 4(2)(-1) = 1 + 8 = 9\). 
Roots:
\[
t = \frac{1 \pm 3}{4}.
\]

So
\[
t = \frac{1 + 3}{4} = 1,\quad t = \frac{1 - 3}{4} = -\frac{1}{2}.
\]

4. Therefore the full factorization is
\[
2t^{3} - 3t^{2} + 1 = (t - 1)^{2}(2t + 1).
\]

So the solutions are 
\[
\boxed{t = 1 \text{ (double root) and } t = -\frac{1}{2}}.
\]

Here’s everything you asked for, kept close to what you need for **Ganita Manjari 9th, Telangana, Ex 5.3**.

---

### 1. Definition of Circle

A **circle** is the set of all points in a plane which are at the **same fixed distance** from a **fixed point**.

- Fixed point → **centre**
- Fixed distance → **radius**

---

### 2. Symmetries of a Circle

A circle has **a lot of symmetry**.

1. **Rotational symmetry** 
- You can rotate a circle by **any angle** (1°, 10°, 90°, etc.) about its centre. 
- It looks exactly the same. 
- So a circle has **infinite rotational symmetry**.

2. **Line symmetry (reflectional symmetry)** 
- Any line passing through the **centre** is an **axis of symmetry**. 
- The circle looks the same on both sides of that line. 
- There are **infinitely many** such lines.

---

### 3. How Many Circles?

Usually this question means:

- Through **three non‑collinear points** in a plane, **only one circle** can be drawn. 

If the three points lie on the same straight line (collinear), **no circle** can pass through all three.

---

### 4. Theorems 1 to 4 
(Chords and the angles they subtend – this is the “up and down and round and round” part.)

These are the standard ones used in your chapter:

#### Theorem 1 
**Equal chords → equal angles at the centre**

If two chords of a circle are **equal in length**, then the **angles subtended at the centre** by these chords are **equal**.

- If \(AB = CD\), then \(\angle AOB = \angle COD\), where \(O\) is the centre.

---

#### Theorem 2 
**Equal angles at the centre → equal chords**

If two angles subtended at the **centre** of a circle are **equal**, then the corresponding **chords are equal**.

- If \(\angle AOB = \angle COD\), then \(AB = CD\).

*(Theorem 1 and 2 are converses of each other.)*

---

#### Theorem 3 
**Equal chords → equal distance from centre**

In the same circle (or congruent circles), **equal chords** are **equidistant from the centre**.

- If \(AB = CD\), then the **perpendicular distances** from the centre to these chords are equal. 
(So, if \(OP \perp AB\) and \(OQ \perp CD\), then \(OP = OQ\).)

---

#### Theorem 4 
**Equal distance from centre → equal chords**

In the same circle (or congruent circles), chords which are **equidistant from the centre** are **equal in length**.

- If \(OP = OQ\) where \(OP \perp AB\) and \(OQ \perp CD\), then \(AB = CD\).

*(Theorem 3 and 4 are also converses of each other.)*

---

### 5. Chords and the Angle They Subtend

A **chord** is a line segment joining **any two points** on the circle.

- If a chord \(AB\) makes an angle at the **centre**, we say it **subtends an angle at the centre**.
- Angle at centre: \(\angle AOB\)
- If the same chord \(AB\) makes an angle at a point on the **circle**, say \(C\), we say it **subtends an angle at the circumference**.
- Angle at circle: \(\angle ACB\)

Important fact used later:

- The angle at the **centre** is **twice** the angle at the **circumference** standing on the **same chord**. 
\[
\angle AOB = 2 \angle ACB
\]

---

### 6. Midpoints and Perpendicular Bisectors of Chords

This is about the relation between the **centre** and **chords**.

1. **Perpendicular from centre to chord bisects the chord** 
- If a line from the centre is **perpendicular** to a chord, it cuts the chord into **two equal parts**. 
- If \(OP \perp AB\) (with \(O\) centre), then \(P\) is the **midpoint** of \(AB\). 
- So, \(AP = PB\).

2. **Line through centre and midpoint of chord is perpendicular to the chord** 
- If \(P\) is the **midpoint** of a chord \(AB\) and \(OP\) joins the centre \(O\) to \(P\), then \(OP\) is **perpendicular** to \(AB\). 
- So, \(OP \perp AB\).

Together, this line is called the **perpendicular bisector** of the chord.

---

\((\text{first bracket}) \times (\text{second bracket})\) and multiply **each term** in the first bracket with **each term** in the second.

1. Multiply \(x\) with each term in the second bracket:
- \(x \cdot \frac{2}{3}x = \frac{2}{3}x^2\)
- \(x \cdot \frac{4}{5}y = \frac{4}{5}xy\)

2. Multiply \(\frac{4}{5}y\) with each term in the second bracket:
- \(\frac{4}{5}y \cdot \frac{2}{3}x = \frac{8}{15}xy\)
- \(\frac{4}{5}y \cdot \frac{4}{5}y = \frac{16}{25}y^2\)

3. Now add all four terms:
\[
\frac{2}{3}x^2 + \frac{4}{5}xy + \frac{8}{15}xy + \frac{16}{25}y^2
\]

4. Combine the middle like terms \(\frac{4}{5}xy\) and \(\frac{8}{15}xy\):

- \(\frac{4}{5} = \frac{12}{15}\), so 
\(\frac{4}{5}xy = \frac{12}{15}xy\)

- \(\frac{12}{15}xy + \frac{8}{15}xy = \frac{20}{15}xy = \frac{4}{3}xy\)

So the final answer is:

\[
\boxed{\frac{2}{3}x^2 + \frac{4}{3}xy + \frac{16}{25}y^2}

ठीक है, अब हम **2 वाला – cosh(α + iβ) वाली identity** को हिंदी में देखते हैं।

---

## Identity क्या है?

जिस identity की बात हो रही है, वह है:

\[
\cosh(\alpha + i\beta) = \cosh\alpha \cos\beta + i\,\sinh\alpha \sin\beta
\]

यह **hyperbolic functions** और **complex numbers** को जोड़ने वाली standard पहचान (identity) है।

---

## ज़रूरी definitions (छोटे में)

1. **Hyperbolic cosine** 
\[
\cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}
\]

2. **Hyperbolic sine** 
\[
\sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}
\]

3. Complex के लिए: 
\[
e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta
\] 
\[
e^{-i\theta} = \cos\theta - i\sin\theta
\]

---

## Identity कैसे निकलेगी? (आसान आइडिया)

1. पहले लिखो:
\[
\cosh(\alpha + i\beta) = \frac{e^{\alpha + i\beta} + e^{-(\alpha + i\beta)}}{2}
\]

2. इसे अलग करो:
\[
= \frac{e^\alpha e^{i\beta} + e^{-\alpha} e^{-i\beta}}{2}
\]

3. अब ऊपर वाले complex formulas लगाओ: 
- \(e^{i\beta} = \cos\beta + i\sin\beta\) 
- \(e^{-i\beta} = \cos\beta - i\sin\beta\)

तो:
\[
e^\alpha(\cos\beta + i\sin\beta) + e^{-\alpha}(\cos\beta - i\sin\beta)
\]

4. अब cosβ और sinβ के साथ terms को जोड़ो–घटाओ, तो real part से 
\[
\cosh\alpha \cos\beta
\] 
और imaginary part से 
\[
i\,\sinh\alpha \sin\beta
\] 
निकलता है।

आख़िर में मिलता है:
\[
\cosh(\alpha + i\beta) = \cosh\alpha \cos\beta + i\,\sinh\alpha \sin\beta
\]

---

अगर तुम चाहो तो मैं अगली बार यही तरीका **सिर्फ steps की list में** और भी छोटा करके दिखा सकता हूँ, या फिर \(\sinh(\alpha + i\beta)\) वाली identity भी समझा सकता हूँ।

| English | Konkani (Roman) |
|---------|------------------|

## **Phrases (no subject + verb)**

### **1) Noun Phrase**
Works like a noun.
- **The tall boy** is my cousin.

### **2) Adjective Phrase**
Describes a noun/pronoun.
- The boy **in the blue shirt** is my brother.

### **3) Adverb Phrase**
Tells how/when/where/why (modifies verb/adjective/adverb).
- He ran **very fast**. (how)
- We met **in the evening**. (when)
- She sat **near the door**. (where)

---

## **Clauses (have subject + verb)**

### **1) Noun Clause**
Acts like a noun (subject/object/complement).
- **What you said** is true. (subject)
- I know **that he is honest**. (object)
- My hope is **that I will win**. (complement)

### **2) Adjective Clause (Relative Clause)**
Describes a noun/pronoun (often starts with *who/which/that/whose/where/when*).
- The girl **who stood first** is my friend.
- This is the pen **which I lost**.
- I met a man **whose car was stolen**.

### **3) Adverb Clause**
Acts like an adverb (time/reason/condition/contrast, etc.).
- I stayed home **because it was raining**. (reason)

**No problem — it sounds like you’re asking “how do I do it?” (and maybe you meant “3×3” or “find”).**

**How to find the cofactor of an entry \(a_{ij}\):**
1. **Choose the entry** (the number) you want the cofactor of.
2. **Cross out its whole row and whole column.**
3. **Look at the smaller matrix left over** and find its **determinant**. That number is the **minor** \(M_{ij}\).
4. **Attach the sign** using this pattern (starts with \(+\) in the top-left):
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
+ & - & +\\
- & + & -\\
+ & - & +
\end{pmatrix}
\]
5. **Cofactor** is:
\[
C_{ij} = (\text{sign})\times M_{ij}
\]

If you send a matrix (even just a 2×2 or 3×3) and tell me which position (like \(a_{1,2}\)), I’ll help you find that cofactor step by step.**

अच्छा सवाल है, चलो वही सवाल दुबारा करते हैं लेकिन \([Ag^+]\) अब **0.0001 की जगह 0.002 M** ले लेते हैं। 

हमारा cell reaction वही है:

\[
\mathrm{Mg(s) + 2Ag^+ (aq) \rightarrow Mg^{2+}(aq) + 2Ag(s)}
\]

दिया है: 
- \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\ \text{V}\) 
- \([\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}] = 0.130\ \text{M}\) 
- \([\mathrm{Ag^+}] = 0.002\ \text{M}\) (नई value) 
- \(n = 2\) (2 इलेक्ट्रॉन ट्रांसफर होते हैं)

25°C पर Nernst equation:

\[
E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.0591}{2}\log Q
\]

### 1. Q निकालते हैं 

\[
Q = \frac{[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2}
= \frac{0.130}{(0.002)^2}
\]

पहले \((0.002)^2\):

\[
0.002 = 2\times10^{-3}
\Rightarrow (0.002)^2 = (2\times10^{-3})^2 = 4\times10^{-6}
\]

अब Q:

\[
Q = \frac{0.130}{4\times10^{-6}}
= \frac{0.130}{4}\times10^{6}
\approx 0.0325\times10^{6}
= 3.25\times10^{4}
\]

### 2. \(\log Q\) निकालते हैं 

\[
\log(3.25\times10^{4})
= \log(3.25) + \log(10^{4})
\]

\[
\log(3.25) \approx 0.512\quad(\text{calculator से})
\]

तो:

\[
\log Q \approx 0.512 + 4 = 4.512
\]

### 3. Nernst equation में डालते हैं 

\[
E_{\text{cell}} = 3.17 - \frac{0.0591}{2}\times 4.512
\]

पहले \(\frac{0.0591}{2}\):

\[
\frac{0.0591}{2} = 0.02955
\]

अब multiply:

\[
0.02955 \times 4.512 \approx 0.1333
\]

अब:

\[
E_{\text{cell}} \approx 3.17 - 0.1333 \approx 3.0367\ \text{V}
\]

लगभग value:

\[
\mathbf{E_{\text{cell}} \approx 3.04\ \text{V}}
\]

यानी जब \([Ag^+]\) को **0.0001 M से बढ़ाकर 0.002 M** किया, तो \(Q\) की value कम हुई, \(\log Q\) भी कम हुआ, और result में **cell potential थोड़ा बढ़कर लगभग 2.96 V से 3.04 V के आसपास** हो गया।

**Question (लगभग ऐसा है):** 
*“Predict / Write about the impact of communication technology on society in a global village.”*

नीचे पॉइंट्स में आसान हिन्दी + थोड़ा English में समझो:

### 1. लोगों को जोड़ देना 
- पहले लोग सिर्फ़ अपने शहर या गाँव तक ही बात कर पाते थे। 
- अब **mobile, internet, video call** से हम दुनिया के किसी भी कोने से बात कर सकते हैं। 
- इससे दुनिया **एक ग्लोबल विलेज / बड़ा गाँव** जैसी लगने लगी है।

### 2. जानकारी जल्दी मिलती है 
- **News, weather, education, online classes** – सब जल्दी मिल जाता है। 
- कोई घटना दुनिया में कहीं भी हो, कुछ ही मिनटों में सबको पता चल जाता है। 
- इससे लोग **ज़्यादा जागरूक (aware)** हो गए हैं।

### 3. व्यापार और नौकरी के मौक़े 
- कंपनियाँ अब अपने देश के अलावा और देशों में भी काम कर सकती हैं। 
- **Online work, freelancing, remote job** जैसी चीज़ें आ गई हैं। 
- इससे कुछ लोगों को नए मौक़े मिले हैं, पर कुछ पुरानी नौकरियाँ भी बदली हैं।

### 4. संस्कृति पर असर 
- अलग‑अलग देशों का **music, movies, fashion, language** आसानी से फैलता है। 
- इससे लोग एक‑दूसरे की **culture को समझते** हैं, लेकिन कभी‑कभी अपनी परंपराएँ कम होती लगती हैं।

### 5. अच्छे और बुरे दोनों असर 
**अच्छे:**
- दूरी कम लगती है 
- सीखना आसान 
- जल्दी मदद मिलती है (जैसे आपदा में, बीमारी में) 

**बुरे:**
- ज़्यादा mobile / internet से **आँखों, दिमाग और रिश्तों** पर असर

- प्राइवेसी (गोपनीयता) का ख़तरा

संचार तकनीक ने समाज को **ज़्यादा जुड़ा हुआ, तेज़ और जागरूक** बना दिया है। 
दुनिया अब **एक global village** जैसी हो गई है, लेकिन हमें इसका **सही और सीमित (responsible)** use करना चाहिए।

- **1 day** has \(24\times 60\times 60 = 86{,}400\) seconds.

\[

\]

A plateau is a large, flat or gently sloping area of land that is higher than the land around it. It is often called a tableland because it looks like a table top raised above the ground.

- Climate controls temperature and rainfall.

## Nucleophilic Substitution Reaction

### 1. Basic Idea
- A **nucleophile** (Nu⁻ or a neutral molecule with a lone pair) attacks a carbon atom.
- It **replaces** another atom or group already attached to that carbon.
- The group that leaves is called the **leaving group** (often a halide like Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻).

**General form:**

- R–X + Nu⁻ → R–Nu + X⁻ 
where 
- R = alkyl group 
- X = leaving group (like Cl, Br, I) 
- Nu⁻ = nucleophile

---

### 2. Nucleophile
- Species that is **rich in electrons** and wants a positive/δ⁺ center.
- Has **lone pairs** or **negative charge**.
- Examples: OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O, RO⁻, I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻.

---

### 3. Leaving Group
- The group that **breaks away** from the carbon with its electron pair.
- Good leaving groups are **weak bases** and stable as ions.
- Examples: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ >> F⁻ (order of leaving ability in many cases).

---

### 4. Types of Nucleophilic Substitution
#### (a) S_N1 (unimolecular)
- Rate depends only on **substrate concentration**.
- Two-step mechanism (via **carbocation**).
- Favoured by:
- 3° > 2° alkyl halides 
- Polar protic solvents (e.g., water, alcohol) 

#### (b) S_N2 (bimolecular)
- Rate depends on **substrate and nucleophile**.
- One-step, **backside attack**, with inversion of configuration.
- Favoured by:
- 1° > 2° alkyl halides 
- Strong nucleophiles, polar aprotic solvents 

---

### 5. Importance
- Used to make **alcohols, ethers, nitriles, amines**, etc.
- Very important in **organic synthesis** and **drug design**.

**3) Find the point on the \(y\)-axis equidistant from \(A(6,5)\) and \(B(-4,3)\).**

Let the required point be \(P(0,y)\) (because it lies on the \(y\)-axis, so \(x=0\)).

Equidistant means \(PA = PB\). Use squares to avoid roots:
\[
PA^2 = PB^2
\]

\[
(0-6)^2 + (y-5)^2 = (0-(-4))^2 + (y-3)^2
\]

\[
36 + (y-5)^2 = 16 + (y-3)^2
\]

Subtract 16 from both sides:
\[
20 + (y-5)^2 = (y-3)^2
\]

Expand:
\[
20 + (y^2 - 10y + 25) = y^2 - 6y + 9
\]

\[
y^2 - 10y + 45 = y^2 - 6y + 9
\]

Cancel \(y^2\) on both sides:
\[
-10y + 45 = -6y + 9
\]

Add \(10y\) to both sides:
\[
45 = 4y + 9
\]

Subtract 9:
\[
36 = 4y
\]

\[
y = 9
\]

So the point is **\(\mathbf{(0,9)}\)**.

**Evolution (विकासवाद) का core idea:** पीढ़ियों के साथ populations (पूरी जनसंख्या) की **heritable** (जीन से आगे जाने वाली) विशेषताओं में बदलाव होता है। यह बदलाव इसलिए टिकता है क्योंकि कुछ बदलाव **survival + reproduction** में मदद करते हैं और कुछ नहीं।

---

## 1) Evolution “क्यों” होता है: Variation कहाँ से आता है?
Evolution के लिए सबसे पहली शर्त है **variation**—यानी एक ही species के individuals एक जैसे नहीं होते। यह variation मुख्यतः 3 कारणों से आता है:

1. **Mutation (जीन/डीएनए में बदलाव):** DNA कॉपी होते समय छोटे changes। 
2. **Recombination (मेयोसिस में mixing):** माँ‑बाप के genes का नया combination बनता है। 
3. **Sexual reproduction:** दो parents होने से हर बच्चा genetically अलग होता है।

**Exam point:** Variation अगर **heritable** नहीं है (जैसे gym से मांसपेशियाँ), तो वह evolution नहीं चलाता। Evolution जीन वाले बदलावों से चलता है।

---

## 2) Natural Selection असल में कैसे काम करता है? (Darwin का मजबूत logic)
Natural selection “nature चुनती है” वाली line नहीं, एक **4-step logic** है:

1. **Overproduction:** organisms जितने बच्चे बनाते हैं, सब survive नहीं कर पाते। 
2. **Struggle for existence:** food/space/साथी/शिकारियों से competition। 
3. **Differential survival & reproduction:** जिनके पास helpful heritable traits हैं, वे ज़्यादा survive करते हैं और ज़्यादा offspring देते हैं। 
4. **Change in gene frequency:** कई पीढ़ियों बाद population में वही trait common हो जाता है।

**यहाँ ध्यान दो:** selection individual को “बदलता” नहीं; selection **population की composition** बदल देता है।

---

## 3) एकदम ठोस उदाहरण (NIOS/board level) — Antibiotic Resistance
ये सबसे exam-relevant और “solid” example है:

- शुरुआत में bacteria की population में **कुछ bacteria** के पास mutation से resistance होता है, बाकी sensitive। 
- Antibiotic देने पर sensitive bacteria मर जाते हैं। 
- Resistant bacteria बचते हैं, तेज़ी से multiply करते हैं। 
- कुछ generations में population mostly resistant हो जाती है।

**Conclusion:** Antibiotic ने resistance “बनाया” नहीं; पहले से मौजूद variation में से resistant वाले **select** हो गए। यही natural selection का असली मतलब है।

---

## 4) “Origin of life” में scientific explanation क्या है? (Chemical Evolution) — facts + flow
NIOS में origin of life के लिए जो scientific frame है, उसका strong version यह है:

1. **Early Earth का environment**: free oxygen बहुत कम/न के बराबर, energy sources बहुत (lightning, UV, volcanoes)। 
2. **Simple molecules से organic molecules:** इन conditions में simple gases से **amino acids जैसे organic molecules** बन सकते हैं। 
3. **Macromolecules → protocells:** organic molecules मिलकर बड़े molecules (proteins, nucleic acids) और फिर membrane जैसी structures में organize हुए। 
4. **First cells:** सबसे पहले बहुत simple cells, जिनकी metabolism/basic replication धीरे‑धीरे improve हुई।

**Evidence वाला point:** Miller–Urey type experiments ने दिखाया कि early-earth जैसी conditions में **simple gases से amino acids** बन सकते हैं—यानी chemical evolution possible है।

---

## 5) Evolution के supporting evidences (कम से कम 4 “पक्के” evidence)
NIOS में evidence अक्सर पूछा जाता है। ये सबसे standard हैं:

1. **Fossils (जीवाश्म):** पुराने layers में simple forms, नए layers में complex forms; transitional forms की idea। 
2. **Homologous organs:** structure same, function अलग (मानव हाथ, whale flipper) → common ancestry का संकेत। 
3. **Analogous organs:** function same, structure अलग (bird wing vs insect wing) → convergent evolution। 
4. **Vestigial organs:** reduced/कम काम वाले अंग (जैसे appendix) → ancestry का clue। 
5. **Molecular evidence:** DNA/protein similarities जितनी ज़्यादा, relationship उतना close।

(Exam में 4 लिखना बोलें तो पहले 4 बहुत safe हैं।)

---

## 6) Classification को evolution से कैसे जोड़ते हैं? (यह हिस्सा अक्सर confused करता है)
Classification सिर्फ नाम रखने के लिए नहीं है; इसका aim है **organisms की evolutionary relationship** दिखाना।

- जो organisms **ज़्यादा traits share** करते हैं (और DNA similarity ज़्यादा), उन्हें closer groups में रखा जाता है। 
- **Species** सबसे specific level: interbreeding करके fertile offspring दे सकें। 
- Hierarchy: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom

**Solid link:** Evolution explains **why** कुछ organisms में similarities हैं (common ancestry), और classification उन similarities के आधार पर **grouping** करता है।

bot_last_message:
We already worked most of this out, so let’s go cleanly step by step and keep it short.

Given:
- \(p(x) = ax + b\)
- \(q(x) = cx + d\)

Conditions:
1. \(p(0) = 5\)
2. \(p(x) - q(x)\) cuts x-axis at \((3, 0)\) → \(p(3) - q(3) = 0\)
3. \(p(x) + q(x) = 6x + 4\) for all real \(x\)

---

**Step 1: Use \(p(0) = 5\)** 
\(p(0) = a\cdot 0 + b = b = 5\) 
So \(b = 5\), hence \(p(x) = ax + 5\).

---

**Step 2: Use \(p(x) + q(x) = 6x + 4\)** 
\(p(x) + q(x) = (ax + 5) + (cx + d) = (a + c)x + (5 + d)\)

Match with \(6x + 4\):

- \(a + c = 6\) 
- \(5 + d = 4 \Rightarrow d = -1\)

So \(q(x) = cx - 1\).

---

**Step 3: Use that \(p(x) - q(x)\) cuts x-axis at \((3, 0)\)** 
At \(x = 3\), 
\(p(3) - q(3) = 0\)

Compute:
- \(p(3) = 3a + 5\)
- \(q(3) = 3c - 1\)

So:
\[
3a + 5 - (3c - 1) = 0
\]
\[
3a + 5 - 3c + 1 = 0
\]
\[
3a - 3c + 6 = 0
\]
\[
3(a - c) = -6 \Rightarrow a - c = -2
\]

Now solve:
\[
\begin{cases}
a + c = 6\\
a - c = -2
\end{cases}
\]

Add them:
\[
2a = 4 \Rightarrow a = 2
\]
Then:
\[
2 + c = 6 \Rightarrow c = 4
\]

---

So:
- \(a = 2, b = 5 \Rightarrow p(x) = 2x + 5\)
- \(c = 4, d = -1 \Rightarrow q(x) = 4x - 1\)

**Final answer: 
\(\boxed{p(x) = 2x + 5,\quad q(x) = 4x - 1}\).**

**ശരി—ഇത് പറ്റിയാൽ കുഴപ്പമുണ്ടാകും. “മൈനസ് ബ്രാക്കറ്റിന് മുന്നിൽ വന്നാൽ അകത്തുള്ള എല്ലാ ചിഹ്നങ്ങളും മാറും” എന്ന ഒരൊറ്റ കാര്യം പിടിച്ചാൽ മതി.**

നമുക്ക് രണ്ട് equation:

\[
(1)\ x+y=26
\]
\[
(2)\ x-y=4
\]

നീ ചോദിച്ചതുപോലെ **(1) − (2)** ചെയ്യാം:

\[
(x+y)-(x-y)=26-4
\]

ഇപ്പോൾ **ഇതാണ് കൺഫ്യൂഷൻ വരുന്ന സ്ഥലം**: 
\(-(x-y)\) എന്നത് **ബ്രാക്കറ്റിനുള്ളിൽ മുഴുവനും sign മാറും** എന്നാണ് അർത്ഥം.

അതായത്:

- \(x\) നു മുന്നിൽ \(+\) ആയിരുന്നു → മൈനസ് വരുമ്പോൾ **\(-x\)**
- \(-y\) ആയിരുന്നു → മൈനസ് വരുമ്പോൾ **\(+y\)**

അതിനാൽ,

\[
-(x-y)=-x+y
\]

ഇത് നേരെ മുൻപത്തെ expression-ലേക്ക് ഇട്ടാൽ:

\[
(x+y)-(x-y)=(x+y)+(-x+y)
\]

ഇപ്പോൾ ചേർത്തെഴുതാം:

\[
x+y-x+y
\]

ഇവിടെ \(x-x=0\) ആയി പോകും:

\[
x-x=0 \Rightarrow y+y=2y
\]

അതിനാൽ ഇടത് വശം:

\[
(x+y)-(x-y)=2y
\]

വലത് വശം:

\[
26-4=22
\]

അതിനാൽ:

\[
2y=22 \Rightarrow y=11
\]

\[
A-(B-C)=A-B+C
\]

ഇവിടെ \(A=x+y,\ B=x,\ C=y\) എന്ന് കരുതിയാൽ:

\[

\]

അതായത് **\( -(-y) = +y\)** ആയത് കൊണ്ടാണ് \(y+y\) വന്നത്.

**मानव प्रजनन (Human Reproduction) का आसान और exam‑ready समझ**

**1) नर जनन तंत्र (Male reproductive system)**
- **वृषण (Testes):** शुक्राणु (sperm) बनते हैं और **टेस्टोस्टेरोन** हार्मोन बनता है। 
- **एपिडिडाइमिस (Epididymis):** शुक्राणु यहाँ mature होकर जमा रहते हैं। 
- **वास डिफरेंस (Vas deferens):** शुक्राणु आगे ले जाने वाली नली। 
- **सहायक ग्रंथियाँ:** 
- **Seminal vesicle, Prostate, Bulbourethral glands** → द्रव बनाती हैं जो मिलकर **वीर्य (semen)** बनाता है; इससे sperm को पोषण और चलने में मदद मिलती है। 
- **लिंग (Penis) / Urethra:** वीर्य बाहर निकलने का रास्ता।

**2) मादा जनन तंत्र (Female reproductive system)**
- **अंडाशय (Ovary):** अंडाणु (ovum) बनते हैं और **एस्ट्रोजन/प्रोजेस्टेरोन** हार्मोन बनते हैं। 
- **अंडवाहिनी (Fallopian tube / Oviduct):** यहीं आम तौर पर **निषेचन (fertilization)** होता है। 
- **गर्भाशय (Uterus):** भ्रूण (embryo) का विकास यहीं होता है। 
- **गर्भाशय ग्रीवा (Cervix) और योनि (Vagina):** birth canal का हिस्सा।

**3) शुक्रजनन (Spermatogenesis) — sperm बनना**
- यह **वृषण की seminiferous tubules** में होता है। 
- क्रम (simple): **spermatogonia → spermatocyte → spermatid → sperm** 
- FSH और LH (ICSH) हार्मोन मदद करते हैं; LH से टेस्टोस्टेरोन बनता है, जो प्रक्रिया को support करता है।

**4) अंडजनन (Oogenesis) — ovum बनना**
- **Oogonia → primary oocyte** (ज्यादातर जन्म से पहले बन जाते हैं) 
- हर menstrual cycle में आम तौर पर **एक** primary oocyte mature होकर **secondary oocyte (ovum बनने की दिशा में)** release होता है (ovulation)।

**5) मासिक धर्म चक्र (Menstrual cycle) — मुख्य बातें**
(औसतन 28 दिन मानते हैं)
- **Menstrual phase (दिन 1–5):** uterine lining टूटकर बाहर आती है (पीरियड्स)। 
- **Follicular/Proliferative phase (दिन 6–13):** follicle बढ़ता है, lining फिर से बनती है; **Estrogen** बढ़ता है। 
- **Ovulation (लगभग दिन 14):** **LH surge** से अंडाणु release होता है। 
- **Luteal/Secretory phase (दिन 15–28):** corpus luteum बनता है, **Progesterone** बढ़ता है; lining pregnancy के लिए तैयार होती है। 
- अगर fertilization नहीं हुआ → progesterone घटता है → फिर से menstruation शुरू।

**6) निषेचन (Fertilization) और भ्रूण विकास**
- निषेचन आम तौर पर **fallopian tube (ampulla region)** में होता है। 
- Fertilized egg = **zygote** → बार-बार division → **morula → blastocyst** 
- **Implantation:** blastocyst का uterus की lining में चिपकना (लगभग 6–7 दिन बाद)। 

**7) प्लेसेंटा (Placenta) — काम**
- माँ और भ्रूण के बीच **खाना/ऑक्सीजन देना** और **अपशिष्ट हटाना**। 
- हार्मोन भी बनाता है (जैसे **hCG, progesterone** आदि — नाम याद रखना useful है)।

**8) प्रसव (Parturition) और स्तनपान (Lactation)**
- प्रसव में uterine contractions से बच्चा बाहर आता है; **Oxytocin** संकुचन बढ़ाने में मदद करता है। 
- **Prolactin** दूध बनवाता है; शुरुआती दूध (colostrum) बच्चे को immunity देता है।

अगर आप चाहें तो मैं **मानव प्रजनन** के 10–12 सबसे important exam questions (सिर्फ topics, full answers नहीं) बता दूँ—या आपको **menstrual cycle / spermatogenesis / placenta** में से किस पर ज़्यादा confusion है?

## 1. Maths – Number System (English Notes)

### 1.1 Types of Numbers

- **Natural numbers (N)** 
Numbers used for counting: 
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …

- **Whole numbers (W)** 
All natural numbers + 0: 
0, 1, 2, 3, 4, …

- **Integers (Z)** 
All positive numbers, negative numbers and zero: 
… –3, –2, –1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …

- **Rational numbers (Q)** 
- Numbers that can be written in the form **p/q**, 
where **p and q are integers** and **q ≠ 0** 
- Examples: 1/2, –3/5, 4 (= 4/1), 0 (= 0/5)

---

### 1.2 Factors and Multiples

- **Factor** 
A number that **divides another number exactly** (without remainder). 
- Example: Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

- **Multiple** 
Numbers we get by **multiplying** a given number with natural numbers. 
- Example: Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, …

- Every number has **many multiples**, but **limited factors**.

---

### 1.3 Prime and Composite Numbers

- **Prime number** 
A number that has **exactly two factors**: 1 and the number itself. 
- Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 
- Important: **2 is the only even prime number.**

- **Composite number** 
A number that has **more than two factors**. 
- Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12

- **Special case** 
- 1 is **neither prime nor composite.**

---

### 1.4 Even and Odd Numbers

- **Even numbers**: Numbers divisible by 2. 
- Examples: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, …

- **Odd numbers**: Numbers **not** divisible by 2. 
- Examples: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …

---

### 1.5 HCF and LCM (Short Summary)

- **HCF (Highest Common Factor)** 
- The **largest common factor** of two or more numbers. 
- Used when we want to **divide things into equal parts** with no remainder.

- **LCM (Least Common Multiple)** 
- The **smallest common multiple** of two or more numbers. 
- Used for questions like: 
- “Two events happening again at the same time.”

- **Biological classification** groups organisms based on **similarities and differences** to make study and identification easier. 
- **Earlier systems** used simple traits (like habitat), but modern classification uses **many characters** (cell type, body organization, reproduction, etc.). 
- **Two-kingdom classification (Plantae/Animalia)** had major problems (e.g., fungi were wrongly grouped with plants; bacteria didn’t fit well). 
- **Whittaker’s Five Kingdom system (1969)** is based mainly on **cell structure, body/thallus organization, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and phylogenetic relationships**. 
- The **five kingdoms** are **Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia**.

**Monera (bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma):**
- **Monerans are prokaryotic**: no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. 
- They can be **autotrophic** (photo/chemo) or **heterotrophic** (saprophytic/parasitic). 
- **Bacteria** show different shapes: **coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum**. 
- **Cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae) are photosynthetic; many form **colonies/filaments** and can fix nitrogen (in some forms). 
- **Mycoplasma** are the **smallest living cells** and **lack a cell wall**.

**Protista:**
- **Protists are mostly unicellular eukaryotes**, often living in water. 
- They include **diatoms, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds, protozoans**. 
- **Diatoms** have silica cell walls (frustules) and contribute greatly to **oxygen production**; deposits form **diatomaceous earth**. 
- **Dinoflagellates** often have two flagella; some cause **red tides**. 
- **Euglenoids** have both plant-like and animal-like features; they have **pellicle** instead of a cell wall. 
- **Protozoans** are heterotrophic protists; some are parasites (e.g., **Plasmodium**).

**Fungi:**
- **Fungi are eukaryotic, heterotrophic** organisms with **absorptive nutrition**. 
- The fungal body is usually made of **hyphae**; a network of hyphae forms **mycelium**. 
- Fungal cell walls are mainly **chitin**. 
- Fungi reproduce by **vegetative methods**, **asexual spores**, and **sexual spores**. 
- Major groups: **Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes, Deuteromycetes** (based on reproductive structures).

**Viruses, viroids, prions (acellular agents):**
- **Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites** and are **inert outside the host cell**. 
- A virus has **nucleic acid (DNA or RNA)** + **protein coat (capsid)**; some have an envelope. 
- **Viroids** are infectious **RNA molecules without a protein coat** (plant pathogens). 
- **Prions** are infectious **proteins** that cause neurodegenerative diseases.

\]

\]

Divide both sides by 2:
\[
l \times b = \frac{2z^3 + 10z^2 + 12z}{2}
= z^3 + 5z^2 + 6z
\]

Now factor \(z^3 + 5z^2 + 6z\):

\[

\]

l \times b = z(z + 2)(z + 3)

Here is a compact proof suitable for board exams.

---

**To prove:** 
\[
\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}
\]

### 1. Single point charge at centre of a sphere

Take a point charge \(+q\) at the centre of a sphere of radius \(r\).

Electric field at distance \(r\) from a point charge:
\[
E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{q}{r^2}
\]

For a small area element \(d\vec{A}\) on the sphere:

- \(\vec{E}\) is radial outward.
- \(d\vec{A}\) is also radial outward.
- Angle between them, \(\theta = 0^\circ\).

So flux through \(d\vec{A}\):
\[
d\phi = \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = E\,dA\cos 0^\circ = E\,dA
\]

Total flux through the whole spherical surface:
\[
\phi = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \oint E\,dA = E \oint dA = E(4\pi r^2)
\]

Substitute \(E\):
\[
\phi = \left(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{q}{r^2}\right)(4\pi r^2)
= \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}
\]

So for a point charge at the centre of a sphere:
\[
\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}
\]

---

### 2. Any closed surface (not just a sphere)

Consider any irregular closed surface enclosing the same charge \(q\).

Draw an imaginary sphere around the charge inside this surface.

- All field lines from \(q\) that pass through the sphere must also pass through the irregular surface.
- Therefore, **number of field lines** crossing both closed surfaces is the same.
- Flux is proportional to number of field lines, so **net flux through both surfaces is the same**.

But flux through the sphere is already:
\[
\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}
\]

Hence flux through any closed surface enclosing \(q\) is also:
\[
\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}
\]

---

### 3. Many charges inside

If the closed surface contains several point charges \(q_1, q_2, \dots\):

- By superposition, \(\vec{E} = \vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2 + \dots\)
- Flux is linear in \(\vec{E}\), so:
\[
\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}
= \oint (\vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2 + \dots)\cdot d\vec{A}
= \oint \vec{E}_1\cdot d\vec{A} + \oint \vec{E}_2\cdot d\vec{A} + \dots
\]

Each term equals \(\dfrac{q_i}{\varepsilon_0}\), so:
\[
\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}
= \frac{q_1}{\varepsilon_0} + \frac{q_2}{\varepsilon_0} + \dots
= \frac{q_1 + q_2 + \dots}{\varepsilon_0}
= \frac{Q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}
\]

So, **proved**:
\[
\boxed{\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}}
\]

If you want, I can now help you with a typical exam question that uses this proof (like field due to a charged sphere or infinite line).

\[
\text{औंस} = \text{पाउंड} \times 16
\]

### **Question 3**

Given \(AD\perp BC\), triangles \(ABD\) and \(ACD\) are right-angled at \(D\).

Using Pythagoras:

\[
AB^2=AD^2+BD^2
\]

Since \(AD^2=BD\cdot CD\),

\[
AB^2=BD\cdot CD+BD^2
\]

\[
AB^2=BD(CD+BD)=BD\cdot BC
\]

Similarly,

\[
AC^2=AD^2+CD^2
\]

\[
AC^2=BD\cdot CD+CD^2
\]

\[
AC^2=CD(BD+CD)=CD\cdot BC
\]

Adding these equations:

\[
AB^2+AC^2=BD\cdot BC+CD\cdot BC
\]

\[
AB^2+AC^2=BC(BD+CD)
\]

Because \(BD+CD=BC\),

\[
AB^2+AC^2=BC^2
\]

By the **converse of Pythagoras’ theorem**, \(\triangle ABC\) is right-angled at \(A\).

\[
\boxed{\angle BAC=90^\circ}
\]

---

### **Question 4**

Given:

\[
\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF
\]

So the corresponding vertices are:

\[
A\leftrightarrow D,\qquad B\leftrightarrow E,\qquad C\leftrightarrow F
\]

Since \(BM\) and \(EN\) are medians:

\[
AM=MC=\frac{AC}{2},\qquad DN=NF=\frac{DF}{2}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{AM}{DN}=\frac{AC}{DF}
\]

From \(\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF\),

\[
\frac{AB}{DE}=\frac{AC}{DF}
\]

Hence,

\[
\frac{AM}{DN}=\frac{AB}{DE}
\]

Also,

\[
\angle BAM=\angle EDN
\]

because \(AM\) lies along \(AC\), and \(DN\) lies along \(DF\), while \(\angle A=\angle D\).

Thus, by **SAS similarity**,

\[
\boxed{\triangle AMB\sim\triangle DNE}
\]

This proves part **(i)**.

For part **(ii)**,

\[
\frac{CM}{FN}=\frac{AC}{DF}
\]

and

\[
\frac{CB}{FE}=\frac{AC}{DF}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{CM}{FN}=\frac{CB}{FE}
\]

Also,

\[
\angle BCM=\angle EFN
\]

because \(\angle C=\angle F\). Hence, by SAS similarity,

\[
\boxed{\triangle CMB\sim\triangle FNE}
\]

This proves part **(ii)**.

From \(\triangle AMB\sim\triangle DNE\), corresponding sides are proportional:

\[
\frac{BM}{EN}=\frac{AM}{DN}
\]

But

\[
\frac{AM}{DN}=\frac{AC}{DF}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\frac{BM}{EN}=\frac{AC}{DF}}
\]

This proves part **(iii)**.

ठीक है, चलो fractions का **add/subtract बिलकुल शुरुआत से** सीखते हैं। तुम अच्छा कर रहे हो जो साफ़‑साफ़ बता रहे हो कि क्या नहीं आता 🙂

---

### 1️⃣ Fraction क्या होता है? (एक बार जल्दी से)

जैसे: 
\(\frac{1}{2}\) मतलब 1 में से 2 बराबर हिस्से, यानी आधा। 
\(\frac{3}{4}\) मतलब 1 में से 4 बराबर हिस्सों में से 3 हिस्से।

ऊपर वाला नंबर = **numerator (ऊपरी भाग)** 
नीचे वाला नंबर = **denominator (नीचे वाला भाग)**

---

### 2️⃣ जब denominator **same हो** (आसान वाला केस)

उदाहरण: 
\(\frac{2}{7} + \frac{3}{7}\)

- दोनों में नीचे 7 है, तो बस **ऊपर के नंबर जोड़ दो** 
\(2 + 3 = 5\) 
तो: \(\frac{2}{7} + \frac{3}{7} = \frac{5}{7}\)

इसी तरह subtraction: 
\(\frac{5}{9} - \frac{2}{9}\)

- नीचे दोनों में 9 है 
- ऊपर: \(5 - 2 = 3\) 
तो: \(\frac{5}{9} - \frac{2}{9} = \frac{3}{9} = \frac{1}{3}\) (जितना हो सके simplify कर देते हैं)

**Rule (jab denominator same हो):** 
बस **ऊपर वाले नंबर add या subtract**, नीचे वाला same रहता है।

---

### 3️⃣ जब denominator **different हो** (थोड़ा important वाला भाग)

मान लो: 
\(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{6}\)

अब नीचे अलग–अलग हैं (4 और 6), तो क्या करें?

**स्टेप 1: नीचे वालों का LCM निकालो** 
- 4 के multiple: 4, 8, 12, 16, … 
- 6 के multiple: 6, 12, 18, … 
Common सबसे छोटा = **12** 
तो नया denominator = **12**

**स्टेप 2: दोनों fractions को denominator 12 में बदलो**

- \(\frac{1}{4}\) को 12 बनाने के लिए: 
4 से 12 तक जाने के लिए \(4 \times 3 = 12\) 
तो ऊपर भी 3 से multiply: 
\(\frac{1}{4} = \frac{1 \times 3}{4 \times 3} = \frac{3}{12}\)

- \(\frac{1}{6}\) को 12 बनाने के लिए: 
6 से 12 तक जाने के लिए \(6 \times 2 = 12\) 
तो ऊपर भी 2 से multiply: 
\(\frac{1}{6} = \frac{1 \times 2}{6 \times 2} = \frac{2}{12}\)

**स्टेप 3: अब दोनों का denominator same है, तो add कर दो**

\[
\frac{3}{12} + \frac{2}{12} = \frac{5}{12}
\]

तो **final answer: \(\mathbf{\frac{5}{12}}\)**

---

### एक subtraction का example भी देख लो

\(\frac{5}{8} - \frac{1}{4}\)

**स्टेप 1: 8 और 4 का LCM**

- 8 के multiple: 8, 16, 24, … 
- 4 के multiple: 4, 8, 12, … 
Common सबसे छोटा = **8**

**स्टेप 2: दोनों को denominator 8 में लिखो**

- \(\frac{5}{8}\) वैसे ही रहेगा \(\frac{5}{8}\) 
- \(\frac{1}{4}\): 4 से 8 तक \(4 \times 2 = 8\) 
तो: \(\frac{1}{4} = \frac{1 \times 2}{4 \times 2} = \frac{2}{8}\)

**स्टेप 3: subtract करो**

\[
\frac{5}{8} - \frac{2}{8} = \frac{3}{8}
\]

तो **answer: \(\mathbf{\frac{3}{8}}\)**

---

### 4️⃣ Rule छोटा सा याद रखने के लिए

1. अगर **denominator same** हो:
- ऊपर वाले नंबर जोड़ो/घटाओ 
- नीचे वाला same रखो 

2. अगर **denominator अलग–अलग** हो:
- नीचे वालों का **LCM** लो 
- दोनों fractions को उस LCM वाले denominator में बदलो 
- फिर ऊपर वाले नंबर add/subtract करो 

---

ठीक है, चलो अध्याय 2 **“रेखिक बहुपद / बहुपद (Polynomials)”** को आसान भाषा में शुरू से समझते हैं। 
मैं इसे छोटे-छोटे हिस्सों में समझाऊँगा:

---

## 1. बहुपद (Polynomial) क्या होता है?

कोई भी ऐसा बीजीय व्यंजक (algebraic expression) जिसमें:
- केवल **घात (powers)** प्राकृतिक संख्या हों (0,1,2,3,…),
- और **भाग में x न हो**, 
उसे बहुपद कहते हैं।

**उदाहरण (बहुपद हैं):**
- \(3x + 5\) 
- \(x^2 + 2x + 1\) 
- \(7\) 
- \(4x^3 - x + 9\)

**उदाहरण (बहुपद नहीं हैं):**
- \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) (क्योंकि x हर में है) 
- \(\sqrt{x}\) = \(x^{1/2}\) (घात पूर्ण संख्या नहीं है) 
- \(x^{-1} + 2\) (घात -1 है, यानी धन पूर्ण संख्या नहीं)

---

## 2. पद (Term), गुणांक (Coefficient), चर (Variable), नियतांक (Constant)

मान लो व्यंजक है: 
\[
4x^2 - 3x + 7
\]

- **पद (Terms)**: \(4x^2\), \(-3x\), \(7\) 
- **चर (Variable)**: \(x\) 
- **गुणांक (Coefficient)**:
- \(4x^2\) का गुणांक = 4 
- \(-3x\) का गुणांक = -3 
- **नियतांक (Constant term)**: 7

---

## 3. बहुपद की घात (Degree)

किसी बहुपद में **x की सबसे बड़ी घात** = उस बहुपद की घात।

**उदाहरण:**
- \(3x + 5\) → सबसे बड़ी घात 1 → degree = 1 
- \(x^2 + 2x + 1\) → सबसे बड़ी घात 2 → degree = 2 
- \(4x^3 - x + 9\) → सबसे बड़ी घात 3 → degree = 3 
- केवल संख्या जैसे 7 → degree = 0 (क्योंकि \(7 = 7x^0\))

---

## 4. घात के आधार पर बहुपद के प्रकार

1. **शून्य बहुपद (Zero polynomial)** 
- हमेशा 0 हो: \(0, 0x, 0x^2\) 
- इसकी degree 9वीं कक्षा में आमतौर पर “परिभाषित नहीं” मानी जाती है।

2. **नियतांक बहुपद (Constant polynomial)** 
- जिसमें x ही न हो, जैसे: 3, -5, 11 
- degree = 0

3. **रेखिक बहुपद (Linear polynomial)** 
- degree = 1, जैसे: \(2x + 3\), \(-x + 5\) 

4. **द्विघात बहुपद (Quadratic polynomial)** 
- degree = 2, जैसे: \(x^2 + 3x + 2\)

5. **घन बहुपद (Cubic polynomial)** 
- degree = 3, जैसे: \(2x^3 - x + 1\)

---

## 5. बहुत ज़रूरी: बहुपद का मान (Value of Polynomial)

अगर बहुपद है \(p(x) = 2x + 3\) 
और तुम्हें x = 4 पर मान निकालना है, तो:

\[
p(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11
\]

यानी, x की जगह जहाँ-जहाँ x है, वहाँ 4 रख दो।

---

## अभी के लिए छोटा सा अभ्यास (खुद से करो)

1. बताओ इनमें से कौन-कौन से बहुपद हैं: 
- (i) \(5x^2 - 3x + 1\) 
- (ii) \(\dfrac{2}{x} + 3\) 
- (iii) \(7\) 
- (iv) \(\sqrt{x} + 1\)

2. इनकी degree निकालो: 
- (i) \(4x^3 - x + 2\) 
- (ii) \(9x + 1\) 
- (iii) \(5\)

An odd number can be written in the form **\(2n + 1\)** (this is what you saw as the “general form” of an odd number).

Now look at numbers ending in 1, 5, and 6.

---

### 1. Numbers ending in 1

Any number ending in 1 has its **units digit = 1**. 
When we square it, the units digit comes from \(1 \times 1\).

\[
1 \times 1 = 1
\]

So the square of any number ending in 1 will also end in **1**.

Example: 
\(21^2 = 441\) → ends in 1 
\(31^2 = 961\) → ends in 1 

**Reason:** units digit 1 squared gives units digit 1.

---

### 2. Numbers ending in 5

Here, the units digit is **5**. 
When we square it, the units digit comes from \(5 \times 5\).

\[
5 \times 5 = 25
\]

So the square of any number ending in 5 will always end in **5** (actually 25, but the units digit is 5).

Example: 
\(15^2 = 225\) → ends in 5 
\(25^2 = 625\) → ends in 5 

**Reason:** units digit 5 squared gives units digit 5.

---

### 3. Numbers ending in 6

Here, the units digit is **6**. 
When we square it, the units digit comes from \(6 \times 6\).

\[
6 \times 6 = 36
\]

So the square of any number ending in 6 will always end in **6**.

Example: 
\(16^2 = 256\) → ends in 6 
\(26^2 = 676\) → ends in 6 

**Final answers:**

- Square of a number ending in **1** ends in **1**. 
- Square of a number ending in **5** ends in **5**. 
- Square of a number ending in **6** ends in **6**.

## 1. What are microorganisms?

- Microorganisms (microbes) are **very tiny living organisms**.
- You **usually need a microscope** to see them.
- Main types:
- **Bacteria**
- **Fungi**
- **Algae**
- **Protozoa**
- **Viruses** (special: show living features only inside a host cell)

---

## 2. Different types (basic idea)

- **Bacteria** 
- Single-celled, very small. 
- Shapes: rod, round, spiral. 
- Some are useful, some are harmful.

- **Fungi** 
- Example: **bread mould**, **yeast**, **mushroom**. 
- Some used in food, some spoil food.

- **Algae** 
- Simple plant-like organisms. 
- Found in water, can be green, brown, red.

- **Protozoa** 
- Animal-like, often live in water or inside other organisms. 
- Some cause diseases.

- **Viruses** 
- Smaller than all others. 
- Can reproduce **only inside** a living cell. 
- Cause many diseases (like common viral fevers).

---

## 3. Microorganisms as **friends**

### (a) In food production

- **Curd from milk:** 
- Bacteria (like *Lactobacillus*) change milk into curd. 
- They turn milk sugar into acids, making it thick and sour.

- **Bread, idli, dosa, etc.:** 
- **Yeast** is used for fermentation. 
- It produces gas bubbles, so the dough rises and becomes soft.

### (b) In medicine

- Some microbes help in making **antibiotics**. 
- Antibiotics are medicines that **kill or stop bacteria**. 
- They do **not** work against viruses.

- Microorganisms are also used to make **vaccines**. 
- A vaccine trains our body to **recognise and fight** a particular disease.

### (c) In agriculture and environment

- **Decomposers:** 
- Microbes break down dead plants and animals. 
- This returns nutrients to the soil.

- **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria:** 
- Some bacteria in soil or in root nodules of leguminous plants (like peas, beans) change nitrogen from air into a form plants can use. 
- This improves soil fertility.

---

## 4. Microorganisms as **foe (harmful)**

### (a) Causing diseases (pathogens)

- Harmful microbes are called **pathogens**. 
- They can cause diseases in:
- **Humans**
- **Animals**
- **Plants**

- They can spread through:
- Air (sneezing, coughing) 
- Water (dirty/contaminated water) 
- Food (spoiled or uncovered food) 
- Direct contact or by insects (like mosquitoes).

### (b) Food spoilage

- When microbes grow on food, they:
- Change its **smell, taste, and colour**. 
- Make it unsafe to eat.

---

## 5. Food preservation (controlling harmful microbes)

Common methods to prevent microbial growth:

- **Refrigeration / freezing:** low temperature slows growth. 
- **Drying:** without water, many microbes cannot grow. 
- **Salting and sugaring:** high salt or sugar stops microbial growth (pickles, jams). 
- **Heating / pasteurisation:** high temperature kills most microbes. 
- **Chemical preservatives:** safe chemicals in small amounts to protect food (your book will give names).

---

## 6. Vaccination and disease prevention

- **Vaccines** prepare the immune system. 
- After vaccination, the body can **quickly fight** that microbe in future.
- Other prevention:
- Clean water 
- Good hygiene 
- Properly cooked food 
- Avoiding open, uncovered food.

**Question 10 is saying:** the *complement* of an angle is **one third** of its *supplement*.

Let the angle be \(x^\circ\).

- The **complement** is what you add to get \(90^\circ\), so it is \(90^\circ - x\).
- The **supplement** is what you add to get \(180^\circ\), so it is \(180^\circ - x\).

Now translate the sentence into an equation:

“Complement is one third of supplement”
\[
90 - x = \frac{1}{3}(180 - x)
\]

Clear the fraction by multiplying both sides by 3:
\[
3(90 - x) = 180 - x
\]

Expand:
\[
270 - 3x = 180 - x
\]

Move the \(x\) terms to one side (add \(3x\) to both sides):
\[
270 = 180 + 2x
\]

Subtract 180:
\[
90 = 2x
\]

Divide by 2:
\[
x = 45^\circ
\]

**So the angle is \(\mathbf{45^\circ}\).** 
(Quick check: complement \(= 90-45 = 45^\circ\), supplement \(= 180-45 = 135^\circ\), and \( \frac{1}{3}\times 135 = 45^\circ\), correct.)

**Irrational numbers:** numbers that **cannot** be written as \(\dfrac{p}{q}\). Their decimals go on forever and **do not repeat any pattern**. Examples: \(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{5}, \pi\).

**Quick checks (the “method”):**
- If it’s an **integer** (…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …) → **rational** (because it’s over 1).
- If the decimal **terminates** (like 2.75) → **rational**.
- If the decimal **repeats** (like \(0.333\ldots\) or \(0.2727\ldots\)) → **rational**.
- If the decimal is **non-terminating and non-repeating** → **irrational**.
- For roots: \(\sqrt{n}\) is **rational** only when \(n\) is a **perfect square** (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, …). Otherwise it’s **irrational**.

---

### 1. सबसे पहले – सिर्फ़ ये समझो

मान लो लिखा है:

\[
x + 3 = 7
\]

इसका मतलब है: **कौन-सा नंबर + 3 करने पर 7 बनता है?**

सोचो: 
4 + 3 = 7 होता है ना? 
तो यहाँ **x = 4**

यानी ये पूरा काम सिर्फ़ “सोच” से भी हो सकता है।

---

### 2. अब वही चीज़ धीर-धीरे तरीके से

\[
x + 3 = 7
\]

यहाँ “+3” x के साथ जुड़ा है। 
अगर इस +3 को हटाना है, तो **उल्टा काम** करेंगे, यानी **–3** करेंगे।

जो भी काम **एक तरफ** करेंगे, **दूसरी तरफ भी वही काम** करना पड़ेगा।

तो:

\[
x + 3 = 7
\]

दोनों तरफ 3 घटाते हैं:

\[
x + 3 - 3 = 7 - 3
\]

अब बाएँ तरफ: \(+3-3 = 0\), तो बचा:

\[
x = 4
\]

बस, जवाब मिल गया: **x = 4**

---

### 3. अब तुम ज़रा सा practice करो

इन तीनों को **सोच कर** करने की कोशिश करो, फिर लिखो कि तुम्हें क्या लगा:

1. \(x + 5 = 9\) → x क्या होगा? 
2. \(x + 10 = 13\) → x क्या होगा? 
3. \(x + 2 = 6\) → x क्या होगा? 

पहले दिमाग़ से सोचो: 
“कौन-सा नंबर + 5 करने पर 9 होगा?” ऐसे।

फिर चाहो तो ऐसे steps भी लिख सकते हो, जैसे मैंने किए:
- दोनों तरफ 5 घटाओ 
- x = ___

---

तुम पहले इनका जवाब लिखो (चाहे सही हो या ग़लत, कोई दिक्कत नहीं), 
फिर अगले step पर चलेंगे — वहाँ पर हम **minus वाले** सवाल देखेंगे, जैसे:

\[
x - 3 = 5
\]

तुम्हारे जवाब देखकर मैं अगला step उतना ही हल्का रखूँगा, जितना तुम्हें आराम से लगे।

\[
x^2 + 3x + 1 = (x - 2)^2
\]

अब इसे हल करते हैं:

1. दाईं तरफ़ का square खोलो: 
\[
(x - 2)^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4
\]

2. अब equation में रखो:
\[
x^2 + 3x + 1 = x^2 - 4x + 4
\]

3. दोनों तरफ़ से \(x^2\) काट सकते हैं:
\[
3x + 1 = -4x + 4
\]

4. अब \(4x\) दोनों तरफ़ जोड़ो:
\[
3x + 4x + 1 = 4
\Rightarrow 7x + 1 = 4
\]

5. अब 1 को दूसरी तरफ़ ले जाओ:
\[
7x = 4 - 1 = 3
\]

6. अब 7 से भाग दो:
\[
x = \frac{3}{7}
\]

**तो \(x\) का मान \(\mathbf{\frac{3}{7}}\) है।**

Here’s a short, clear summary of **both rise and fall** of the Delhi Sultanate.

---

## 1. Rise of the Delhi Sultanate

- After **Prithviraj Chauhan** was defeated by **Muhammad Ghori** (Second Battle of Tarain, 1192), northern India became open to Turkish control. 
- Ghori’s general **Qutbuddin Aibak** became ruler in Delhi and founded the **Mamluk (Slave) dynasty** in **1206**. This is the **start of the Delhi Sultanate**. 
- The Sultans built a strong **army**, used **horsemen and archers**, and collected **land revenue** to maintain power. 
- Different dynasties expanded their territory:
- **Mamluk (Slave) dynasty** – set up rule in Delhi. 
- **Khalji dynasty** – Alauddin Khalji expanded to Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Deccan, and controlled prices and markets. 
- **Tughlaq dynasty** – Muhammad bin Tughlaq tried new ideas like shifting the capital and token currency (many failed, but he ruled a very large empire). 

Because of these rulers, **Delhi became the political center** of a large part of north India.

---

## 2. Fall / Decline of the Delhi Sultanate

The Delhi Sultanate slowly became weak due to many reasons:

1. **Too many weak rulers** 
- After strong Sultans, many later rulers were weak and could not control nobles and provinces.

2. **Rebellions and powerful regional kingdoms** 
- Governors and local chiefs started acting **independently**.

bot_last_message:
Differentiate implicitly:
\[
\sin^2 y+\cos(xy)=x
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dx}(\sin^2 y)+\frac{d}{dx}(\cos(xy))=\frac{d}{dx}(x)
\]

First term (chain rule):
\[
\frac{d}{dx}(\sin^2 y)=2\sin y\cos y\;\frac{dy}{dx}
\]

Second term: \(\frac{d}{dx}(\cos u)=-\sin u\;u'\) with \(u=xy\).
\[
\frac{d}{dx}(xy)=y+x\frac{dy}{dx}
\]
So,
\[
\frac{d}{dx}(\cos(xy))=-\sin(xy)\left(y+x\frac{dy}{dx}\right)
\]

Put it together:
\[
2\sin y\cos y\;\frac{dy}{dx}-\sin(xy)\left(y+x\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=1
\]

Expand and collect \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) terms:
\[
2\sin y\cos y\;\frac{dy}{dx}-y\sin(xy)-x\sin(xy)\frac{dy}{dx}=1
\]
\[
\left(2\sin y\cos y-x\sin(xy)\right)\frac{dy}{dx}=1+y\sin(xy)
\]

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1+y\sin(xy)}{2\sin y\cos y-x\sin(xy)}}
\]

You can also write \(2\sin y\cos y=\sin(2y)\), giving
\[
\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1+y\sin(xy)}{\sin(2y)-x\sin(xy)}}
\]

ठीक, ab hum **α (alpha) और β (beta)** ko simple language mein samjhte hain. 
Yeh topic 10th class ke **quadratic equations** chapter mein aata hai.

---

## 1. Alpha (α) aur Beta (β) kya hote hain?

Agar koi quadratic equation ho:

\[
ax^2 + bx + c = 0 \quad (a \neq 0)
\]

Iske **do roots** (solutions) hote hain. Unhi roots ko hum naam de dete hain:

- पहला root = **α (alpha)**
- दूसरा root = **β (beta)**

Bas, α aur β sirf **naam** hain roots ke. Jaise hum bol dein:
- “Is equation ke roots 2 aur 3 hain”
ya 
- “Is equation ke roots α aur β hain”

---

## 2. Important formulas (bahut use hote hain)

Agar equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) ke roots **α aur β** hain, to:

1. **Sum of roots (योग):**
\[
\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}
\]

2. **Product of roots (गुणनफल):**
\[
\alpha \beta = \frac{c}{a}
\]

Yahi formulas practice set 1.5 mein baar‑baar use hote hain.

---

## 3. Chhota sa example (sirf idea ke liye)

Equation: 
\[
x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0
\]

Yahan:
- \(a = 1\)
- \(b = -5\)
- \(c = 6\)

To:

- \(\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac{b}{a} = -\dfrac{-5}{1} = 5\) 
- \(\alpha \beta = \dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{6}{1} = 6\)

Iska matlab:
- Dono roots ka **sum = 5**
- Dono roots ka **product = 6**

(Actual roots 2 aur 3 hain, aur सच में 2 + 3 = 5, 2 × 3 = 6)

---

Questions आमतौर पर aise hote hain:

- Diya hota hai: equation, aur pucha hota hai 
**α + β, αβ, α² + β², α²β + αβ²** etc. nikalna
- Ya kabhi kabhi **sum aur product** diye hote hain, aur equation banाने को bolते hain.

Isliye pehle tumhe yeh **do formulas** pakke se yaad hone chahiye:
- \(\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac{b}{a}\)
- \(\alpha \beta = \dfrac{c}{a}\)

---

**कदम 1: विपरीत मान लो** 
मान लो \(3 + 2\sqrt{5}\) परिमेय है। 
तो इसे किसी परिमेय संख्या \(r\) के बराबर लिख सकते हैं:

\[

\]

\[
\sqrt{5} = \frac{r - 3}{2}
\]

दाएँ तरफ \(\dfrac{r - 3}{2}\) दो परिमेय संख्याओं का भाग है, 
इसलिए \(\dfrac{r - 3}{2}\) भी **परिमेय** होगी।

For now, here’s a bit more explanation for **both** (still keeping it exam-level).

**Q1 (Myopia, far point 2 m): why \(v=-2\) m and why power is negative** 
- A myopic eye can’t see very far; the farthest clear point is the **far point = 2 m**. 
- To see a distant object (taken as at **infinity**), the correcting lens must create a **virtual image** of that distant object **at the far point**, so the eye can focus it. 
- A **virtual image** formed on the same side as the object is taken as **negative**, so \(v=-2\ \text{m}\). 
- For \(u=-\infty\), \(\frac{1}{u}\approx 0\), so \(\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}\Rightarrow f=-2\ \text{m}\). 
- Negative \(f\) means a **concave (diverging) lens**, so power is also **negative**: 
\[
P=\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{-2}=-0.5\ \text{D}
\] 
**Final:** **–0.5 D concave lens**

**Q2 (Angular dispersion): what it means** 
- A prism bends different colours by different amounts because each colour has a different refractive index in glass. 
- **Violet deviates more** than red, so the spread between them tells you how much the prism “separates” colours. 
- Angular dispersion is defined (in this level) as: 
\[
\delta_v-\delta_r = 42^\circ-38^\circ = 4^\circ
\] 
**Final:** **4°**

Here’s a simple way to see the difference:

### 1. Union / Central Government
- Means the **same thing** in India: **Union government = Central government**. 
- Governs the **whole country** (all states and union territories). 
- Handles **national subjects**, like:
- Defence (Army, Navy, Air Force) 
- Foreign affairs 
- Railways 
- Currency and banking 

### 2. State Government
- Governs **only one state** (like Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, etc.). 
- Handles **state-level subjects**, like:
- Police (law and order in the state) 
- Public health and hospitals (mostly) 
- Agriculture 
- State roads 

So:
- **Union/Central** = whole of India 
- **State** = one particular state within India

## 1. Double-angle (just remember these 3)

**Core Pythagoras:** 
\[
\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1
\]

**a) \(\sin 2\theta\)** – super important 
\[
\boxed{\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta}
\] 
Pattern: “sin double = 2 × sin × cos”

**b) \(\cos 2\theta\)** – remember only ONE, derive others 
Best to fix this one in memory:
\[
\boxed{\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta}
\]

From this + \(\sin^2+\cos^2=1\), you can quickly get:

- \(\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1\) 
- \(\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\)

So only **one** needs to be memorised.

**c) \(\tan 2\theta\)** – use sin/cos 
\[
\tan 2\theta = \dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{\cos 2\theta}
= \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}
\] 
Pattern: “2tan on top, 1 − tan² below”.

---

## 2. Triple-angle (only if needed)

Just the **standard ones**:

\[
\boxed{\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta}
\]

\[
\boxed{\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta}
\]

They look similar: coefficients **3–4** and **4–3**.

---

## 3. Power-reduction (helpful in integration)

These just come from cos 2θ:

From \(\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\):
\[
\boxed{\sin^2\theta = \dfrac{1-\cos 2\theta}{2}}
\]

From \(\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1\):
\[
\boxed{\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2}}
\]

Pattern: 
- sin² → 1 **minus** cos2θ, over 2 
- cos² → 1 **plus** cos2θ, over 2

**6) Dividing a quantity in a ratio (Q6)** 
If something is divided in ratio \(1:4\):
